title: Performance and debugging
summary: The single-threaded event loop and its O(N) hazards, the SLOWLOG / LATENCY / INFO / MONITOR toolbox, common latency sources, pipelines, and MULTI-EXEC-WATCH transaction semantics.

blocks.body:
Redis executes commands on **one main thread**. Networking is multiplexed and,
since Redis 6, socket reads/writes can be parallelized by I/O threads — but
command execution itself is serialized. That single fact explains most Redis
performance behavior, and the exam leans on it heavily: the whole instance is
only as fast as its slowest command, and every client waits behind it.

## Why O(N) commands stall everyone

A well-chosen command finishes in microseconds. An O(N) command against a
million-element collection holds the event loop for the entire scan — every
other client's request queues behind it. The recurring offenders:

- `KEYS *` over a large keyspace.
- `SMEMBERS` / `HGETALL` / `LRANGE 0 -1` / `ZRANGE 0 -1` on huge collections.
- `SINTER` / `SUNION` across large sets, `SORT`, `BITCOUNT` on a huge string.
- `DEL` of a big key — memory reclamation on the main thread (use `UNLINK`).

The habit the exam rewards: for any command, ask "what is N here, and how big
can N get in production?" — then reach for a cursor variant (`SSCAN`, `HSCAN`,
`ZSCAN`, `SCAN`), a `LIMIT`, or an incremental delete strategy.

## SLOWLOG: what ran slow

SLOWLOG is an in-memory ring buffer of commands that exceeded a threshold — no
disk I/O, negligible overhead, per-instance.

```redis
CONFIG SET slowlog-log-slower-than 1000   # microseconds, default 10000 (10 ms)
CONFIG SET slowlog-max-len 256            # entries kept, default 128
SLOWLOG GET 10                            # newest entries first
SLOWLOG LEN
SLOWLOG RESET
```

Each entry records the command's arguments, duration in microseconds, timestamp,
and client address. Two limits to remember: it logs the command, not the root
cause (a slow `GET` may be a swap stall, not a big collection), and it only
captures commands that crossed your threshold — set the threshold before the
incident, not after.

## LATENCY: the latency framework

SLOWLOG answers "which commands were slow"; the LATENCY command family answers
"which *server events* caused latency spikes". Enable monitoring, then query:

```redis
CONFIG SET latency-monitor-threshold 100   # milliseconds
LATENCY HISTORY fork                       # every spike of this event
LATENCY LATEST                             # most recent event per type
LATENCY DOCTOR                             # analysis + recommendations
LATENCY RESET                              # clear the events log
```

Events are named after their cause — `fork` (a save or rewrite forked and stalled),
`aof-fsync`, `expire-cycle`, `eviction-cycle`, fast/slow command buckets. Two
exam-grade correlations: `fork` spikes track `bgsave` / AOF rewrite timing, and
`LATENCY DOCTOR` is the canned first-read when an operator asks "why did latency
spike at 03:00?".

## INFO: the instrument panel

`INFO` reports grouped metrics; the exam focuses on four sections:

- `stats` — throughput and work: `instantaneous_ops_per_sec`,
  `total_commands_processed`, `keyspace_hits` / `keyspace_misses` (hit ratio for
  cache questions), `evicted_keys`, `expired_keys`, `rejected_connections`, and
  `latest_fork_usec` (how long the last `bgsave`/rewrite fork stalled).
- `memory` — `used_memory_human`, `used_memory_rss`, `mem_fragmentation_ratio`
  (ratio well above ~1.5 suggests fragmentation), and whether
  `mem_allocator` is jemalloc.
- `commandstats` — per-command aggregates: `cmdstat_get:calls=1234,usec_per_call=3`
  — the fastest way to see which command family dominates latency.
- `keyspace` — per-database `keys`, `expires`, `avg_ttl`.

`INFO all` is the usual first look during an incident: throughput, hit ratio,
memory pressure, and fork cost in one call.

## MONITOR: powerful, and a production hazard

`MONITOR` streams every command the server processes, live. Invaluable for
reproducing a client bug — and dangerous: the server formats and fans out every
command's traffic to the monitoring connection **on the main thread**, which can
cut throughput by a large factor and grow the output buffer unboundedly.
Debug locally or on a replica; never leave it running in production.

## Where latency actually comes from

- **Swap**: if the OS pages Redis memory out, every access pays disk latency.
  Keep Redis memory within RAM, watch `used_memory_rss` vs `used_memory`, avoid
  swapping at all costs — Redis docs are blunt about this.
- **Fork**: `bgsave` and AOF rewrite fork the process; fork duration scales with
  memory pressure and pages written, and stalls the main thread for its duration
  (`latest_fork_usec`). Huge instances fork slower.
- **Big deletes and big scans**: `DEL` of a multi-GB key, `KEYS`, `SMEMBERS` —
  prefer `UNLINK` and cursor commands.
- **AOF fsync**: with `appendfsync always`, every write waits for the disk.
- **Eviction and expiry**: hitting `maxmemory` triggers eviction cycles; a
  backlog of expiring keys lengthens the expire cycle.
- **Network**: saturated bandwidth, client output-buffer limits, many small
  round trips (fix with pipelining).

## Pipelines: batch the round trips

A pipeline sends many commands in one write and reads the replies as one batch.
The server still executes them one at a time — pipelining saves the *network
round trips*, not execution:

```text
3 commands, no pipeline: 3 × RTT
3 commands, pipelined:   1 × RTT  (often ~10x throughput on distant clients)
```

Bulk ingest, cache warming, and metric flushes are the natural fits. Caveats:
the server queues replies until the whole batch is consumed, so a pipeline of
millions of commands pressures memory on both ends — chunk batches (hundreds to
thousands), and pipelines are **not** transactions: nothing is atomic, and other
clients' commands can interleave between yours.

## MULTI / EXEC / WATCH: transactions without rollback

```redis
MULTI
INCR counter:orders
LPUSH audit:orders "order-42"
EXEC
```

`MULTI` switches the connection to queueing; `EXEC` runs everything queued,
serially and atomically — no other client's command interleaves. Semantics the
exam drills:

- **Queueing errors** abort the transaction: a command with wrong arity or
  unknown name fails the whole thing; `EXEC` returns an error and nothing runs.
- **Execution errors do not roll back** anything. If the third queued command
  fails at runtime (wrong type, say), the first two stay applied and the fourth
  still runs. Redis has **no rollback**: the reasoning is that failed commands
  come from programming bugs, not runtime races, and rolling back adds
  complexity with no practical recovery path.
- **`WATCH key`** is optimistic locking: `EXEC` fails (returns nil) if any
  watched key changed between `WATCH` and `EXEC` — the check-and-set idiom for
  read-modify-write races. `UNWATCH` cancels; `DISCARD` flushes the queue and
  leaves the transaction.

For multi-step logic that must decide based on values it reads, Lua scripts
(`EVAL`) execute atomically too — and can branch, unlike transactions.

## Exam takeaways

- Command execution is single-threaded and serialized; one O(N) command stalls
  every client, so always ask how big N can get.
- SLOWLOG catches slow commands in a bounded in-memory ring; LATENCY ties
  spikes to server events (`fork`, `aof-fsync`, eviction); `LATENCY DOCTOR`
  interprets them.
- `INFO stats` carries hit ratio and evictions, the `persistence` section
  reports `latest_fork_usec`; `commandstats` ranks commands by cost;
  `keyspace` counts keys and TTLs.
- `MONITOR` streams all traffic and can crater production throughput.
- Pipelines batch round trips, not execution; transactions queue and run
  atomically, but execution errors never roll back — pair `WATCH` with
  `EXEC` for check-and-set.
